title: Megacities: real AQA questions
sub: An optional extra for Week 3. Every question below is from a real AQA GCSE Geography paper (Paper 2, Urban issues and challenges). About 20 minutes on screen, then the written paper.
skill: Use the figure, add a named example, then make a judgement.
target: AQA caps many answers at a lower level if you ignore the figure. Quote a number or a detail from it, then add your own case-study fact.

blocks.q: A city grows because more babies are born than people die there. What is this called?
blocks.why: Natural increase = births minus deaths. The other main cause of city growth is rural-urban migration.

blocks.q: “Better-paid jobs in factories in the city.” Is this a push or a pull factor?
o: Push: it drives people away from the countryside
Pull: it attracts people to the city
blocks.why: Pull factors attract people to the city. Push factors drive them out of rural areas (e.g. drought, few jobs).

o: Lagos has a population of over 15 million.
Overall, the opportunities matter more than the problems, because jobs are what bring people to the city in the first place.
There is a lot of traffic in megacities.
blocks.why: A judgement compares and decides, and gives a reason (overall… because…).

sections.sub: Study each figure before answering. Open the mark scheme after each one.

blocks.q: Which statement completes the following sentence? A megacity is a city with at least…
blocks.why: A megacity has at least 10 million people.

points.t: The increasing proportion / percentage of the population living in towns and cities (accept ‘in urban areas’)

mark.note: AQA: no credit for “an increasing number or size of cities” or “the population growing”. The key word is proportion: a bigger share of people live in towns and cities.

blocks.stem: Study Figure 1, a world map showing cities expected to become megacities by 2050.

fig.alt: World map of emerging megacities with 2022 and projected 2050 populations in millions: Chicago 8.9 to 10.8; London 9.6 to 10.8; Baghdad 7.6 to 13.0; Tehran 9.4 to 10.6; Khartoum 6.2 to 11.2; Ahmedabad 8.5 to 13.0; Surat 7.9 to 12.0; Pune 7.0 to 10.8; Chengdu 9.5 to 10.6; Nanjing 9.5 to 10.4; Ho Chi Minh City 9.1 to 13.0; Nairobi 5.2 to 10.4; Dar es Salaam 7.5 to 16.4; Luanda 9.0 to 14.6.
fig.label: June 2025, Paper 2, Figure 1

blocks.q: Which continent is expected to have the most new megacities in 2050? Shade one circle only.
blocks.why: Count them. Asia: Baghdad, Tehran, Ahmedabad, Surat, Pune, Chengdu, Nanjing, Ho Chi Minh City = 8. Africa: Khartoum, Nairobi, Dar es Salaam, Luanda = 4.

blocks.q: What is the expected percentage growth of Nairobi 2022–2050? Shade one circle only.
blocks.why: Nairobi goes from 5.2 to 10.4 million. The increase is 5.2 million, which is the same as the starting size, so it is a 100% increase (it doubles). 200% would mean it trebles.

blocks.q: Give one reason for the growth of megacities in LIC/NEEs.

points.t: Any one of: (high rates of) rural-urban migration · (high rates of) natural increase · urban and industrial development concentrated in one or two large cities · primate cities that grow into megacities

blocks.stem: Study Figure 2, some data about three of the cities shown in Figure 1.
blocks.q: Suggest how natural increase and migration affect the growth of LIC/NEE cities. Use Figure 2 and your own understanding.

levels.d: Limited understanding of how natural increase and/or migration affect growth. Limited use of Figure 2.
Clear understanding of how natural increase and migration affect urban growth, with some reference to Figure 2.

mark.note:
AQA: maximum Level 1 if you do not refer to Figure 2.
What examiners look for: a low median age means many young people of child-bearing age, so many children are born (natural increase); thousands more people per week shows very fast growth (you can turn 3850 a week into about 550 a day, or 200 000 a year); a young population supplies workers but puts pressure on housing and services; growth of informal settlements.

blocks.html: Print the written paper. It has a real 6-mark “to what extent” question with a photograph. You need your Week 3 case-study card (your megacity and its facts). The mark scheme is on the last page.

items: I used a number or detail from the figure in every longer answer.
I wrote proportion for urbanisation, not just “more people”.
I named a real city with a specific fact.
My longer answer ends with a judgement: overall… because…

blocks.q: “Khartoum’s median age is 20. Why does that make the city grow faster?”
blocks.note: For the parent: listen for “lots of young adults → lots of babies → natural increase”.

paper.title: Geography Week 3 plus: megacities (written)
paper.sub: Ember · Real AQA GCSE Geography question (Paper 2) · about 20 minutes · have your Week 3 case-study card ready
paper.intro: Skill: figure + named example + judgement. AQA’s mark scheme gives a maximum of Level 2 if you use only the photo or only your example. Use both, then decide how far.

blocks.stem: Study Figure 3, a photograph of a street class run by volunteers in Mexico City.

fig.alt: A street class in Mexico City: children sit at small desks on a pavement next to parked cars and a lorry, with volunteers helping them and a pile of books.
fig.label: June 2023, Paper 2, Figure 3

blocks.q: To what extent has urban growth created social opportunities? Use Figure 3 and a LIC/NEE example you have studied.

cols: My case study: city and one specific fact

selfcheck: I used a detail from the photo (e.g. the class is on the street, run by volunteers).
I named my case-study city and gave a specific fact (a number, a place, a project).
I explained how urban growth creates the opportunity (education, health, jobs).
I showed a limit: not everyone gets it, or it is informal.
I finished with a judgement: “to a large extent / to some extent… because…”.

marking.h: AQA mark scheme: June 2023, Q01.6 (6 marks)
marking.html:
• Level 3 (5–6, detailed): detailed understanding of the relationship between urban growth and the opportunities offered; thorough analysis of the figure and another example.
  • Level 2 (3–4, clear): clear understanding of the relationship; some analysis of the figure and/or another example.
  • Level 1 (1–2, basic): limited understanding; limited analysis of the figure and/or another example.
Max Level 2 if you used only Figure 3, or only your own example.

What examiners credit: the informal nature of some education and the existence of schooling even if small (from the photo); volunteer teachers; children can attend school where none were available in the rural areas they migrated from (e.g. 68% secondary education in Lagos versus 60% primary in rural northern Nigeria); projects with an education element (e.g. the floating school in Makoko, Lagos); job training (e.g. the Favela Bairro scheme); better water supply in cities (e.g. 75% in Lagos versus 42% in rural Nigeria), so fewer water-borne diseases; strong sense of community (e.g. Dharavi, Mumbai); jobs, even informal ones, only if linked to better food, housing or education.
